fields.sample_size: 10 primary schools (7 public, 3 private) in Rumphi town, Malawi, January to July 2016: structured observations at all ten; interviews with 23 students with a disability, 11 teachers and 2 government stakeholders
fields.legal_measurement_quality: moderate (the policy framework is described by the authors, not tested: National Sanitation Policy 2008, National Water Policy 2005, the 2006 disability equalisation policy, and the statement that the Disability Act 2012 does not make inclusive WASH provision legally binding; interviewees were asked about practice, awareness and consultation, not about the law)
fields.effect_estimate: No school had facilities that fully met the needs of students with disabilities and private schools were not necessarily better: no school had an access ramp or supporting rails to the water source, 70% had uneven paths, only one (a public school) had a dedicated accessible latrine, and all latrine doors were under 1 m wide. About half (11 of 23) of the students described problems accessing drinking water and more than half (13 of 23) problems with the sanitation facilities; 10 of 23 reduced food and drink intake to avoid using the latrines. Adapting existing sanitation facilities to the WHO standard would cost on average MK54,000 (USD 78; range MK28,000 to MK74,600). The authors name four barriers between policy and practice: expert gaps in private schools, limited training and hierarchy for special-needs teachers, a narrow medical model of disability with no consultation of students, and no national standards or monitoring.

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a qualitative and observational study of ten schools in one Malawian town; read in full text 2026-10-04.
pdf_note: Journal copy (University of Louisville repository, 16 pages) read in full from Drive file S403_Zaunda_H_2018...pdf; tables were read as text
notes: CORRECTION of the earlier extraction: it said interviewees (government officials) confirmed the Disability Act is not legally binding and that there is no monitoring; the paper states this itself (introduction and discussion) and does not report interviewees saying it. The legal measurement quality is lowered from high to moderate accordingly.
